article.headline: The Gigawatt AI Data Center and Its Borrowed Arithmetic
article.lede: On May 10, David Sacks — co-founder of Craft Ventures and the man who spent fifteen months as Trump's White House AI czar — posted a four-line calculation claiming that a one-gigawatt AI data center costs $50 billion to build, generates $25–30 billion in annual revenue, and pays for itself in two years. The post drew two million impressions and 578 replies. One of his four figures holds up cleanly; the other three require conditions no independent analyst treats as a baseline.
article.body:
David Sacks — co-founder of Craft Ventures, co-host of the *All-In* podcast, and the man who spent fifteen months shaping American AI policy as Trump's White House AI czar — posted four lines on May 10 that drew 578 replies and two million impressions. **A one-gigawatt AI data center** costs about $50 billion to build, generates $25–30 billion in annual revenue, and pays itself back in two years, he wrote. The boom, he concluded, is real.

The $50 billion figure is not Sacks's own arithmetic — it is Nvidia (NVDA) chief executive Jensen Huang's. Huang has told investors that each gigawatt of AI data-center capacity represents “$40–50 billion in revenue to Nvidia,” and Barclays (BARC.L) analysts have specifically labeled this “Jensen Math,” estimating it overstates Nvidia's actual per-gigawatt take by $7–10 billion. Independent estimates cluster lower: Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon puts all-in construction at roughly $35 billion per gigawatt, breaking it down as 39% GPUs, 33% civil and electrical infrastructure, and 13% networking; McKinsey's model, which projects $5.2 trillion in global data-center investment through 2030, implies approximately $41 billion. Sacks chose the top of the reported range as his starting number.

The revenue line is the most contested figure. A gigawatt of AI compute running current *GB200 NVL72* racks at roughly 120 kilowatts each powers approximately 460,000–500,000 Blackwell-generation GPUs, once cooling and distribution losses are accounted for — a ratio captured by the metric *power usage effectiveness*, or PUE. To produce $25–30 billion annually from that hardware requires near-peak *GPU-hour* pricing, near-continuous utilization, or both simultaneously: reaching $25 billion at 75% utilization implies an average realized rate of about $7.60 per GPU-hour, achievable for committed enterprise contracts at today's Blackwell pricing but not a market baseline. H100 spot rates have already fallen 64% from their 2024 peak as more than 300 new GPU cloud providers entered the market; similar compression in the Blackwell generation would erode this figure sharply in years two and three. Conservative models built from wholesale *colocation* rates and enterprise cloud contracts suggest $10–15 billion per gigawatt-year. Amazon (AMZN)'s AWS, the world's largest cloud provider, generates roughly $3.7–4.3 billion in revenue per gigawatt of capacity it operates, though its workload mix spans far more than pure AI inference.

The electricity estimate — $1–2 billion per year — is the one figure that checks out cleanly. At the US commercial average of roughly 14 cents per kilowatt-hour, running one gigawatt continuously for a year costs about $1.24 billion; operators with *power-purchase agreements* in low-cost states can push that below $800 million. What the tweet omits is everything else in the operating stack — labor, cooling, networking, software, hardware refresh — which cloud operators typically run at 15–25% of revenue. Even accepting Sacks's revenue assumptions and computing operating profit generously, the all-in payback runs to roughly 2.3–3 years at best. At moderate utilization or with any price compression factored in, the horizon extends to four or five. Ratings agency S&P Global (SPGI) wrote in early 2026 that the lag between AI capital expenditure and profit “will remain elevated for an extended period”; Goldman Sachs (GS) structures its own trillion-dollar buildout models around multi-year returns. No independent analyst consensus supports two years as a median expectation.

None of this makes the buildout notional. Microsoft (MSFT), Meta (META), Amazon (AMZN), and the Stargate consortium — OpenAI, SoftBank (9984.T), and Oracle (ORCL) — are collectively committing roughly $725 billion in data-center capital expenditure in 2026 alone; the first genuine gigawatt-scale facilities are being energized this year in Memphis, Abilene, and rural Louisiana. But Sacks is not a neutral observer. He returned to Craft Ventures in March 2026 after exhausting his 130-day *Special Government Employee* appointment, during which his firm retained more than 400 investments in AI-adjacent companies and received two separate ethics waivers. Senate investigators documented a $22 million Craft Ventures investment in Vultron — an AI company targeting federal procurement contracts — made while Sacks was in office. His tweet faithfully reproduces Nvidia (NVDA)'s own gigawatt economics, a narrative whose primary commercial beneficiary is Nvidia itself. The electricity figure is accurate. The rest is best read as a promotional document.

concepts.definition: Nvidia's current flagship rack-scale AI computing module, housing 72 Blackwell B200 GPUs in a dense, liquid-cooled chassis. Each rack draws approximately 120 kilowatts and is designed for large-scale AI training and inference at data-center scale. The NVL72 designation indicates 72 GPUs connected via Nvidia's NVLink fabric within a single rack unit.

A ratio measuring data-center energy efficiency: total facility power input (including cooling, lighting, and power conversion losses) divided by the power actually delivered to IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 is theoretically perfect; real-world AI data centers typically run 1.2–1.4, meaning 20–40% of input power is consumed before it ever reaches a GPU.

The standard unit for pricing rented GPU compute time: one GPU running for one hour. Cloud providers charge per GPU-hour, and market rates shift sharply with supply and demand. A fleet of 500,000 GPUs running at 75% utilization for a year produces roughly 3.3 billion billable GPU-hours; the realized revenue per hour is the central variable in Sacks's contested projection.

A data-center business model in which the facility operator provides physical space, electrical power, and cooling infrastructure while tenant companies own and operate their own servers and networking hardware. Colocation rates are quoted per kilowatt per month and are far lower per kilowatt than what a hyperscaler earns running its own compute cloud, because the software margin and utilization risk stay with the tenant.

A long-term contract — typically 10–20 years — between an electricity generator and a large industrial buyer, fixing the price of power at rates negotiated below prevailing market levels. Major data-center operators use PPAs, often for renewable energy, to stabilize operating costs and reduce exposure to spot-market price volatility.

A US federal appointment category for temporary advisers and consultants, capped by law at 130 working days per calendar year. SGEs face narrower financial-disclosure and ethics-recusal requirements than permanent federal employees, a distinction that critics argued allowed Sacks to retain his VC portfolio while setting AI policy his investments stood to benefit from.

article.fact_check: Sacks presents his figures as moderate back-of-envelope estimates, but each number is drawn from the optimistic end of its range or beyond. The $50 billion capex figure originates in Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's investor presentations, not independent analysis; Bernstein puts the figure at $35 billion per gigawatt and McKinsey implies approximately $41 billion. The $25–30 billion annual revenue projection requires 75%-plus GPU utilization sustained at near-peak Blackwell pricing, in a market that saw H100 spot rates collapse 64% from peak as supply expanded. The two-year payback is not supportable under any independent analyst base-case model; S&P Global Ratings and Goldman Sachs both frame the current AI capex cycle around multi-year return horizons. Only the $1–2 billion electricity cost estimate is consistent with independent data.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_amzn.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
ticker_amzn.blurb: Amazon operates the world's largest e-commerce marketplace and the leading cloud infrastructure platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS). AWS generates the majority of Amazon's operating profit despite representing a minority of total revenue. The company also has significant positions in digital advertising, streaming (Prime Video), and logistics infrastructure. Amazon is a major investor in AI, both through AWS cloud AI services and through a multi-billion-dollar strategic stake in Anthropic.
ticker_amzn.recent: Amazon reported FY2025 revenue exceeding $650 billion, with AWS growing at roughly 17% annually and crossing $100 billion in run-rate revenue. The advertising segment has become a meaningful profit contributor. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026), with the stock gaining approximately 10% over that period — the weakest performer in the Pelosi 2026 exercise batch.

ticker_spgi.name: S&P Global Inc.
ticker_spgi.blurb: S&P Global Inc. is a leading provider of financial intelligence, credit ratings, benchmarks, and analytics. Its core divisions include S&P Global Ratings (one of the world's three major credit rating agencies), S&P Global Market Intelligence (data and research platforms), S&P Global Commodity Insights, and S&P Dow Jones Indices, which administers the S&P 500 and thousands of other indices. The company significantly expanded its scale through the 2022 merger with IHS Markit, reinforcing its position as a critical infrastructure provider for global capital markets.
ticker_spgi.recent: Shares fell approximately 4.15% on May 13, 2026, closing at $406.55 — a notable single-day decline that prompted coverage on MarketBeat asking why the stock dropped, though the specific catalyst is not detailed in available sources. Pre-market pricing on May 14 showed a modest recovery to $407.97, suggesting the sell-off may be stabilizing. Not enough public information from these sources to confirm the precise earnings or macro trigger behind the move.

Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_meta.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
ticker_meta.blurb: Meta Platforms, headquartered in Menlo Park, California, operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — collectively the largest social-media ecosystem in the world by monthly active users. The company generates the vast majority of its revenue through digital advertising, using detailed behavioural data to target ads across its platforms. After a painful 2022 in which shares fell roughly 65% amid a revenue slowdown and ballooning metaverse losses, Meta executed a dramatic turnaround by cutting costs, boosting margins, and rapidly integrating AI-driven ad ranking tools (Advantage+) that demonstrably improved advertiser returns. CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared 2023 a 'Year of Efficiency' and the company followed through. By late 2025 Meta was simultaneously the most profitable it had ever been and the most aggressive in AI infrastructure spending, committing up to $65 billion in capex for 2025 and raising that figure to as much as $145 billion for 2026.
ticker_meta.recent: Meta reached an all-time high near $796 per share in September 2025. The stock declined approximately 24–28% from that peak through April 2026, with the primary investor concern being the scale of the 2026 capital-expenditure commitment — up to $145 billion — and uncertainty about whether AI-driven revenue would materialise at the pace required to justify it. Quarterly earnings remained strong through the period, but multiple compression drove share-price weakness.

ticker_orcl.name: Oracle Corporation
ticker_orcl.blurb: Oracle is an enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company founded by Larry Ellison in 1977 and headquartered in Austin, Texas. Its core businesses are database software (Oracle Database remains the dominant enterprise RDBMS by revenue), cloud applications (ERP, HCM, and CX via Oracle Fusion and NetSuite), and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), its IaaS platform. OCI entered the AI infrastructure race later than AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud but has emerged as a preferred hyperscale partner for OpenAI and other large AI workloads, partly due to competitive GPU pricing and multi-region data-centre commitments. Oracle is an equity participant in the Stargate joint venture alongside OpenAI and SoftBank.
ticker_orcl.recent: Oracle's fiscal Q3 2026 (ending February 2026) was described by management as the strongest quarter in more than 15 years: total revenue rose 22% year-on-year to $17.2 billion, cloud revenue jumped 44% to $8.9 billion, and GPU-related cloud revenue grew 177% year-on-year in the prior quarter. The company reported a $523 billion remaining performance-obligation backlog — driven by AI mega-deals with OpenAI and Meta — and committed approximately $50 billion in capital expenditure for fiscal 2026. BNP Paribas analysts estimated that Oracle's 4.5 gigawatt Stargate capacity commitment could eventually generate $30–60 billion in annual revenue.

poster_davidsacks.blurb: David Sacks is a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and venture capitalist best known as a founding PayPal executive (COO/product) and a member of the so-called PayPal Mafia. He founded Yammer, an enterprise social network acquired by Microsoft in 2012 for ~$1.2B, and later co-founded Craft Ventures, a VC firm focused on SaaS and crypto. He is a co-host of the high-profile All-In Podcast alongside Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and David Friedberg, and was appointed by President Trump as the White House AI & Crypto Czar in January 2025.
poster_davidsacks.credibility_note: Sacks has a strong track record as an operator and early-stage investor. He holds a pronounced libertarian/conservative political outlook and publicly endorsed Trump ahead of the 2024 election, which colors his commentary on regulation, AI policy, and crypto. His dual role as a sitting government official and active podcast commentator is a noted conflict-of-interest concern raised by critics.
